Wild Camping in Scotland: The Rules for Riders

Scotland is unique in the UK — wild camping is a legal right under the Land Reform (Scotland) Act 2003, often called the Right to Roam. For motorcycle tourers, this means you can camp for free across most of the Scottish landscape. But this right comes with responsibilities. Here's what you need to know.

The Legal Position

The Scottish Outdoor Access Code gives everyone the right to camp on most unenclosed land, provided you:

  • Camp in small numbers
  • Stay only 1-2 nights in any one spot
  • Leave no trace — remove all litter and evidence of your stay
  • Avoid camping in enclosed fields with crops or livestock
  • Don't camp next to buildings or in someone's garden (obviously)
  • Take care near roads and lochs — some popular areas have seasonal restrictions

Where You CAN Wild Camp

  • Open hillsides and moorland
  • Beside lochs (except restricted zones like Loch Lomond seasonal bylaws)
  • In woodland and forest (away from buildings)
  • Beaches (above the high tide line)
  • Lay-bys and road verges (technically grey area — some tolerated, some not)

Where You CANNOT Wild Camp

  • Enclosed fields with livestock or crops
  • Private gardens and grounds
  • Some areas around Loch Lomond and The Trossachs National Park (seasonal camping management zones — check current bylaws)
  • Sites of Special Scientific Interest if camping would cause damage

Motorcycle-Specific Considerations

As a motorcycle tourer, wild camping has some unique considerations:

  • Parking your bike: You need somewhere flat and firm to park your motorcycle. Soft ground near lochs can be problematic — carry a small plate or piece of wood to prevent the side stand sinking.
  • Security: A disc lock and cover provide basic security. In truly remote areas, your bike is unlikely to be disturbed, but peace of mind matters for a good night's sleep.
  • Arriving discreetly: Wild camping works best when you're subtle. Arrive in the evening, leave in the morning. Don't make a spectacle of yourself.
  • Noise: A motorcycle engine at 10pm is not subtle. Coast the last few hundred metres if approaching a camping spot near others.
Leave No Trace is not a suggestion — it's the foundation of the right to wild camp. If everyone leaves their rubbish, lights fires irresponsibly, and damages the land, the right will be restricted. Protect it by respecting it.

Best Areas for Motorcycle Wild Camping

  • Northwest Highlands: Vast, empty, and stunning. Countless spots beside lochs and on hillsides. The area between Ullapool and Durness is wild camping paradise.
  • Cairngorms: Ancient pine forests and mountain scenery. Plenty of spots in Glen Feshie and around Loch Morlich.
  • Scottish Borders: Quieter and more accessible. Rolling hills and river valleys with easy-to-find camping spots.
  • Skye: Spectacular but popular. Find spots away from the main tourist areas — the Trotternish peninsula has excellent options.

Essential Wild Camping Kit

  • Tent with good waterproofing (Scottish weather can change fast)
  • Sleeping bag rated to at least 5°C (colder at altitude)
  • Self-inflating mat for comfort and insulation
  • Water purification (filter or tablets — stream water is everywhere but needs treating)
  • Midge repellent and head net (June-September — essential)
  • Trowel for responsible toilet use (bury waste, carry out toilet paper)

Wild camping in Scotland is one of Europe's great freedoms. Use it wisely and you'll experience the Highlands in a way that no hotel guest ever can.
keyTakeaways: Wild camping is a legal right in Scotland under the Land Reform (Scotland) Act 2003, the Right to Roam.
Camp in small numbers, stay only 1-2 nights in one spot, and leave absolutely no trace.
Loch Lomond and The Trossachs National Park has seasonal camping management byelaws, so check current rules.
Carry a plate or wood to stop your side stand sinking on soft ground near lochs.
Midge repellent and a head net are essential from June to September.

faq.q: Is wild camping legal in Scotland?
faq.a: Yes. Under the Land Reform (Scotland) Act 2003 and the Scottish Outdoor Access Code, everyone has the right to camp on most unenclosed land. You must camp in small numbers, stay only one or two nights in any one spot, avoid enclosed fields with crops or livestock, keep away from buildings, and leave no trace of your stay.

faq.q: Are there any areas where wild camping is restricted?
faq.a: Yes. Parts of Loch Lomond and The Trossachs National Park have seasonal camping management byelaws that require permits or ban camping in certain zones, so always check the current rules before you go. Sites of Special Scientific Interest should also be avoided where camping would cause damage.

faq.q: How do I park a motorcycle when wild camping?
faq.a: You need somewhere flat and firm. Soft ground near lochs can swallow a side stand, so carry a small metal plate or piece of wood to spread the load. Arrive discreetly in the evening and leave in the morning, and coast the last stretch if you are near other campers, because a motorcycle engine at 10pm is anything but subtle.

faq.q: What kit do I need for wild camping in Scotland?
faq.a: A well-waterproofed tent, a sleeping bag rated to at least 5C, a self-inflating mat, and water purification for stream water. From June to September midge repellent and a head net are essential. Carry a trowel for responsible toileting, burying waste and carrying out toilet paper, and keep a disc lock and cover for basic bike security.
